article.headline: Light, Memory, and the Question of Lateness
article.lede: A six-word recommendation, posted to a six-figure follower count, points at four names already up multiples this year: Sivers Semiconductors, Lumentum, Applied Optoelectronics, and Micron. The thesis is the AI build-out's two physical bottlenecks, optics and memory. Whether it is in fact 'not too late' depends on what one believes about hyperscaler capex through 2027 and how much of that belief is already in the price.
article.body:
The four tickers @MacnBTC has stitched together share a single underlying claim: that the buildout of AI data centres has shifted the binding constraint away from compute silicon and onto two adjacent layers, the optical interconnects that move data between accelerators and the high-bandwidth memory that feeds those accelerators. Each name plays a different role in that story.

Lumentum (LITE) is the headline beneficiary. The company makes lasers and optical components that go into the high-speed transceivers (the small modules that convert electrical signals to light and back) wired into AI clusters. In March 2026 Nvidia disclosed a roughly $2 billion strategic investment in Lumentum, paired with a similar commitment to Coherent Corp, intended to lock in supply for the multi-year build-out of co-packaged optics. Q2 2026 earnings showed revenue up about 65% year over year, and management has indicated that production is sold through 2027. Even so, the stock now trades on a forward price-to-earnings multiple in the 60s against an industry median around 23, and at roughly seven times next-twelve-months sales. The fundamentals are real; the multiple bakes in flawless execution.

Applied Optoelectronics (AAOI) is the higher-beta version of the same trade. It is a smaller, historically volatile transceiver maker that has converted from a multi-year struggle into hyperscaler design wins, including a single 1.6T transceiver order reported above $200 million and 800G orders above $124 million from another customer. Management is guiding to roughly $1 billion of revenue in 2026, more than double 2025. Capacity is expected to scale from about 90,000 800G units per month at end-2025 toward 500,000 across 800G and 1.6T by end-2026. The market cap, around $14 billion, prices that ramp aggressively; the 52-week low under $13 is a reminder of what mis-execution looks like in this name.

Sivers Semiconductors (SIVE) is the speculative leg. The Swedish-listed photonics specialist makes the indium-phosphide laser chips that sit inside transceivers and, increasingly, inside the external light source modules used in co-packaged optics. Recent partnerships with Jabil on a 1.6T module and with O-Net and Enablence on AI-datacentre light sources point at the right addressable market. It is, however, a small-cap with limited revenue today, and most of the thesis is forward-looking.

Micron (MU) is the memory leg. High-bandwidth memory, or HBM, is the stacked DRAM that sits beside an AI accelerator and feeds it data fast enough to keep its tensor cores busy; HBM3E is the current generation, HBM4 the next. Micron began mass production of HBM4 in early 2026 for Nvidia's Vera Rubin platform, has stated its 2026 HBM capacity is sold out under binding contracts, and posted Q2 2026 revenue near $24 billion with non-GAAP gross margin around 75%. The firm has approved roughly $25 billion in fiscal-2026 capex and a 30% dividend increase. Of the four, Micron has by far the best earnings-multiple discipline, with a forward P/E in the high single digits on consensus, reflecting residual scepticism that the memory cycle has structurally changed.

Is it too late? The honest answer is that the operating story is not over: hyperscaler capex commitments stretch into 2027, the 800G-to-1.6T transition favours the incumbents in the basket, and HBM contracts have lengthened from quarterly to multi-year. Two cautions are worth stating. First, valuations on the optical names already discount most of that. Second, co-packaged optics — Nvidia's stated direction — is a longer-dated disruption to today's pluggable transceiver vendors; the pluggable architecture should dominate through 2027, but the architecture-shift risk is not theoretical. The basket is a coherent expression of a coherent thesis. It is also a late-cycle one.

concepts.definition: A small pluggable module that converts electrical signals into modulated light and back, allowing high-speed data to travel over fibre between switches, servers, and accelerators in a data centre.

Successive generations of optical-interconnect data rates, expressed in gigabits or terabits per second per port. AI clusters are migrating from 400G to 800G and into 1.6T to keep up with bandwidth between GPUs.

Stacks of DRAM chips bonded vertically and placed adjacent to an AI accelerator, connected by a wide interface that delivers far more bandwidth than conventional memory. HBM3E is the current generation; HBM4 is shipping in 2026.

An architecture that integrates optical engines directly into the same package as a switch ASIC or GPU, replacing pluggable modules. CPO offers large power savings and is being championed by Nvidia, with broad deployment expected in 2027 and beyond.

A separate laser unit that feeds light into co-packaged optics modules, allowing the lasers (the most heat-sensitive component) to sit outside the hot accelerator package. Sivers is one of the suppliers pursuing this architecture.

The annual capital expenditure of the largest cloud and AI buyers — Amazon, Microsoft, Google, Meta and a few others — on data-centre infrastructure. It is the single largest demand input for both optical interconnects and HBM.

article.fact_check: All earnings, capex, and order figures are reported by company filings, press releases, or major financial outlets covered in sources. One search result quoted Micron's market cap at '$5 trillion'; that is not consistent with reported share count and price and was disregarded. Forward P/E figures vary across sources because of rapid price moves; ranges are used.

ticker_sive.name: Sivers Semiconductors AB (publ)
ticker_sive.blurb: Sivers designs and manufactures indium phosphide (InP) distributed feedback lasers and optical amplifiers used inside high-speed optical transceivers, automotive LiDAR systems and satellite communications terminals. Its photonics business is one of the few independent western sources of the laser dies that go into AI-data-centre optical links, alongside larger incumbents such as Coherent and Lumentum. A separate wireless unit supplies 5G millimetre-wave RF chips. The company has been preparing a spin-off and potential dual Nasdaq New York listing of its photonics subsidiary.
ticker_sive.recent: Shares ran from roughly SEK 4 at the start of 2026 to a close of SEK 55.95 in early May, a year-to-date gain of about 1,247%, on customer wins including a 1.6T linear-drive optical module collaboration with Jabil announced 15 April 2026 and a LiDAR ramp scheduled for Q4 2026 with up to $138m of cumulative lifetime revenue. 2025 net sales were SEK 304m (+25% YoY) but the after-tax loss was SEK 186m, prompting an April 2026 directed issue of 8.62m shares at SEK 14.50 raising about SEK 125m at roughly 2.5% dilution. Photonics experts and Swedish business media have publicly questioned whether the rally has run ahead of fundamentals.

sources.title: Sivers Semiconductors: a co-packaged optics, LiDAR and SATCOM play
Photonics experts question Sivers Semiconductors' share rally

ticker_lite.name: Lumentum Holdings Inc.
ticker_lite.blurb: Lumentum makes the lasers, optical chips, and components that go into the high-speed transceivers wiring AI data centres together. Spun out of JDSU in 2015, it spent its first decade as a 3D-sensing and telecom-optics supplier of moderate growth. The AI-cluster build-out has remade it into one of the principal upstream beneficiaries of hyperscaler capex, alongside Coherent Corp.
ticker_lite.recent: Q1 fiscal-2026 set record revenue, with management citing AI-driven demand and an order book that runs into 2027. In March 2026 Nvidia announced a roughly $2 billion strategic investment paired with multi-year purchase commitments for co-packaged-optics components. The company joined the S&P 500 in March 2026; shares have surged on AI demand, leaving the stock at a forward P/E in the 60s, materially above peers.

ticker_aaoi.name: Applied Optoelectronics, Inc.
ticker_aaoi.blurb: Applied Optoelectronics is a Texas-based maker of optical components and transceivers, historically known for serving cable-television networks and a handful of hyperscale customers in cycles of feast and famine. The AI build-out has dragged it firmly into the data-centre supply chain, where it now competes for 400G, 800G, and 1.6T transceiver volumes against Lumentum, Coherent, Innolight, and Eoptolink.
ticker_aaoi.recent: Management is guiding to full-year 2026 revenue exceeding $1 billion, more than double 2025's roughly $456 million, on the back of 800G ramps and a single 1.6T order disclosed at over $200 million. The company aims to scale from roughly 90,000 800G units per month at end-2025 toward 500,000 800G/1.6T units per month by end-2026. The stock hit an all-time high near $192 in early May 2026, having traded as low as $12.56 within the last 52 weeks.

ticker_mu.name: Micron Technology, Inc.
ticker_mu.blurb: Micron is the only US-headquartered manufacturer of DRAM and NAND memory at scale, competing with Samsung and SK Hynix. Historically the most cyclical of the three, it has spent the past two years repositioning toward high-bandwidth memory (HBM), the stacked DRAM that pairs with AI accelerators, where pricing is multiples of standard DDR5 and contracts are multi-year rather than spot.
ticker_mu.recent: In March 2026 Micron began mass production of HBM4 12-Hi 36GB stacks for Nvidia's Vera Rubin platform; management has stated 2026 HBM capacity is sold out under binding agreements. Fiscal Q2 2026 revenue was around $23.9 billion, with non-GAAP gross margin near 75%. The board approved a 30% dividend increase and roughly $25 billion of fiscal-2026 capex. Despite a strong year-to-date move, the forward P/E remains in the high single digits on consensus, reflecting residual cyclicality scepticism.

poster_macnbtc.name: MacnBTC
poster_macnbtc.blurb: A trading-focused account active on X since May 2018, with a follower count in the high hundreds of thousands. The byline is 'Mac' and the avatar a wolf; content centres on chart-based trade ideas across both crypto and US equities, including past calls on Bitcoin macro levels, altcoins (SOL, MATIC), and large-cap stocks (TSLA, AAPL).
poster_macnbtc.recent: The bookmarked tweet recommends a basket of AI-infrastructure names — Sivers Semiconductors (SIVE), Lumentum (LITE), Applied Optoelectronics (AAOI), and Micron (MU) — accompanied by screenshots showing strong daily moves and a single line: 'still not too late to buy these btw.' The account historically promotes free trading content rather than paid groups, and its style leans short and chart-driven rather than analytical.
poster_macnbtc.credibility_note: MacnBTC is a personality-led trading account, not a research shop. Calls are short-form and lack the company-level financial analysis or risk caveats one would expect from a sell-side note. The four names selected are real and the underlying AI-optics/memory thesis is mainstream; the question of 'too late' is a judgement call the tweet does not engage with.
